prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- Some of Zimbabwe's children are "wasting away" as political turmoil and economic crisis have caused a severe food shortage, according to a report from Save the Children. Children sleep in rough conditions on the border between Zimbabwe and South Africa. The number of acute child malnutrition cases has risen by almost two-thirds in the past year, the report from the UK-based agency said in its appeal to world donors for help. "There is no excuse for failing to provide this food," program director Lynn Walker said. "The innocent people of Zimbabwe should not be made to suffer for a political situation that is out of their control." Five million Zimbabweans -- out of a population of about 12 million -- are in need of food aid now, the report said. The group is appealing for 18,000 tons of food for next month. "We have already been forced to reduce the rations of emergency food we are delivering because there isn't enough to go around," the report said. "If, as we fear, the food aid pipeline into Zimbabwe begins to fail in the new year the millions of people who rely on emergency food aid will suffer." Zimbabwe is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since its independence from Great Britain 28 years ago. There is an acute shortage of all essentials such as cash, fuel, medical drugs, electricity and food. President Robert Mugabe blames the crisis on the sanctions imposed on him and his cronies by the West for allegedly disregarding human rights. But Mugabe's critics attribute the crisis to his economic policies. As the economy has faltered for almost a decade now, a cholera epidemic is raging, fueled by the collapse of health, sanitation and water services in Zimbabwe. The epidemic has claimed more than 1,100 lives and infected more than 20,000 people since its outbreak in August. Health experts have warned that the water-borne disease could infect more than 60,000 unless its spread is halted. The political crisis rose to a boil in this year when the opposition party claimed that it won the presidential election, but Mugabe's government refused to recognize the result. Instead, the race was thrown to a runoff, which was boycotted by the opposition. Mugabe signed an agreement with the opposition in September to form a unity government, but a bitter dispute over the division of cabinet seats has prevented its formation. Inflation is so severe that the government was forced to print $10 billion currency notes last week, with each expected to buy just 20 loaves of bread.

outputs.L1:
**HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) —** Some of Zimbabwe’s children are “wasting away” as political turmoil and an economic crisis have created severe food shortages, according to a report by Save the Children.

Children are sleeping in harsh conditions along the border between Zimbabwe and South Africa. Cases of acute child malnutrition have risen by almost two-thirds over the past year, the UK-based agency said in an appeal for help from international donors.

“There is no excuse for failing to provide this food,” program director Lynn Walker said. “The innocent people of Zimbabwe should not be made to suffer for a political situation that is out of their control.”

Five million Zimbabweans—out of a population of approximately 12 million—are now in need of food aid, the report said. The organization is appealing for 18,000 tons of food for next month.

“We have already been forced to reduce the rations of emergency food we are delivering because there isn’t enough to go around,” the report said. “If, as we fear, the food aid pipeline into Zimbabwe begins to fail in the new year, the millions of people who rely on emergency food aid will suffer.”

Zimbabwe is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since gaining independence from Great Britain 28 years ago. The country is experiencing acute shortages of essential resources, including cash, fuel, medical drugs, electricity and food.

President Robert Mugabe blames the crisis on sanctions imposed by the West against him and his cronies for allegedly disregarding human rights. Mugabe’s critics, however, attribute the crisis to his economic policies.

As the economy continues a decline that has lasted nearly a decade, a cholera epidemic is raging, fueled by the collapse of Zimbabwe’s health, sanitation and water services. Since the outbreak began in August, the epidemic has claimed more than 1,100 lives and infected more than 20,000 people. Health experts have warned that the waterborne disease could infect more than 60,000 people unless its spread is halted.

The political crisis reached a boiling point this year when the opposition party claimed victory in the presidential election, but Mugabe’s government refused to recognize the result. Instead, the election proceeded to a runoff, which the opposition boycotted.

Mugabe signed an agreement with the opposition in September to form a unity government, but a bitter dispute over the allocation of Cabinet seats has prevented its formation.

Inflation is so severe that the government was forced to print $10 billion currency notes last week, each of which was expected to buy just 20 loaves of bread.

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) — Save the Children has warned that political instability and economic collapse have created such serious food shortages in Zimbabwe that some children are becoming dangerously emaciated. Some youngsters are also sleeping in harsh conditions near the Zimbabwe–South Africa border.

In an appeal to international donors, the UK-based organization reported that cases of acute malnutrition among children had increased by nearly two-thirds over the previous year.

“There is no justification for not supplying this food,” said program director Lynn Walker. “Ordinary Zimbabweans should not be punished for political circumstances beyond their control.”

According to the report, approximately 5 million people in Zimbabwe—whose total population is around 12 million—currently require food assistance. Save the Children is seeking 18,000 tons of food for the coming month.

The agency said it had already had to cut the emergency rations it distributes because supplies were insufficient. It also cautioned that, if the flow of food aid into Zimbabwe breaks down in the new year as feared, millions who depend on emergency provisions will face severe hardship.

Zimbabwe is experiencing its gravest economic and humanitarian emergency since gaining independence from Britain 28 years earlier. Basic necessities—including money, fuel, medicines, electricity, and food—are all in critically short supply.

President Robert Mugabe has said the crisis is the result of Western sanctions imposed on him and his close associates over accusations that they ignored human rights. His opponents, however, argue that Mugabe’s own economic policies are responsible.

After almost a decade of economic decline, Zimbabwe is also confronting a major cholera outbreak, worsened by the failure of the country’s healthcare, sanitation, and water systems. Since the epidemic began in August, more than 1,100 people have died and over 20,000 have been infected. Public-health specialists have warned that the waterborne illness could affect more than 60,000 people if it is not contained.

The political confrontation intensified during the year after the opposition asserted that it had won the presidential election, a result Mugabe’s administration declined to accept. A runoff was then scheduled, but the opposition refused to participate.

In September, Mugabe and the opposition signed a power-sharing deal intended to establish a unity government. Its creation has been blocked, however, by a fierce disagreement over how cabinet positions should be allocated.

Inflation has reached such extreme levels that the government printed $10 billion banknotes the previous week, each of which was expected to purchase only about 20 loaves of bread.

Save the Children has appealed to international donors for 18,000 tons of food, warning that any breakdown in aid deliveries could place millions of lives at risk.

Responsibility for the crisis remains disputed: government officials have blamed international sanctions, while critics argue that damaging economic policies and political mismanagement are the principal causes.

At the same time, the deterioration of the country’s health, sanitation, and water systems has fueled a major cholera epidemic. More than 1,100 people have died, and over 20,000 infections have been officially recorded. Health authorities and aid organizations have warned that the outbreak could ultimately affect more than 60,000 people unless clean water, sanitation, medical treatment, and humanitarian assistance are restored quickly.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about Zimbabwe’s humanitarian crisis, focusing on child malnutrition, food shortages, cholera, hyperinflation, and political turmoil under Robert Mugabe.
counterfactuals.output:
**Zimbabwe’s children bear the brunt as hunger, disease and political turmoil deepen**

**HARARE, Zimbabwe —** In clinics across Zimbabwe, health workers weigh children whose thin arms and swollen stomachs reveal the toll of a national crisis.

Years of food shortages, economic collapse and political upheaval under President Robert Mugabe have left millions struggling to secure basic necessities. Aid agencies warn that children are among the most vulnerable, with acute malnutrition rising in communities where families survive on one meal a day — if they eat at all.

The breakdown of commercial agriculture, drought and government land policies have contributed to steep declines in food production. Once regarded as a regional breadbasket, Zimbabwe has become heavily dependent on imported grain and international food aid.

At the same time, hyperinflation has rendered salaries and savings nearly worthless. Prices can rise between a worker’s morning commute and the trip home, while shops often lack bread, cooking oil and other staples. The government has repeatedly issued bank notes in ever-larger denominations, but cash remains scarce and many transactions have shifted to foreign currency or barter.

The collapse of public services has also fueled a deadly cholera epidemic. Broken water systems, overflowing sewage and shortages of medicine have allowed the disease to spread rapidly through crowded urban areas and rural communities. During the 2008-2009 outbreak, the World Health Organization recorded more than 98,000 suspected cases and over 4,000 deaths.

Hospitals have struggled to operate without reliable electricity, clean water, equipment or adequately paid staff. Many doctors and nurses have left the country, joining an exodus of Zimbabweans seeking work and security elsewhere in southern Africa.

The humanitarian emergency is unfolding against a backdrop of political turmoil. Mugabe, in power since independence in 1980, faced mounting domestic and international criticism after the disputed 2008 elections. Opposition supporters reported widespread intimidation and violence, while opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai withdrew from the presidential runoff, saying his supporters were being targeted.

A power-sharing agreement eventually made Tsvangirai prime minister, but deep mistrust remained, and Mugabe retained control over key state institutions.

The government has blamed Western sanctions, drought and foreign interference for Zimbabwe’s decline. Critics say years of economic mismanagement, corruption, political repression and chaotic land seizures drove the country toward collapse.

For families searching for food and clean water, however, the political arguments offer little relief. Aid workers say immediate access to nutrition, sanitation and medical care is essential — especially for children, for whom even a short period of severe hunger can cause lasting harm.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a news article dated around late 2008 describing Zimbabwe’s worsening economic and humanitarian conditions, including the cholera outbreak, disputed election, stalled unity government, and new $10 billion banknotes.
counterfactuals.output:
**Zimbabwe Crisis Deepens as Cholera Spreads and New $10 Billion Note Is Issued**

*HARARE, Zimbabwe — December 19, 2008*

Zimbabwe’s economic and humanitarian crisis worsened this week as a cholera epidemic spread across the country, political leaders remained deadlocked over a power-sharing government, and the central bank introduced a $10 billion banknote that is barely enough to cover basic purchases.

The cholera outbreak, blamed largely on the collapse of water, sanitation and health services, has killed more than 1,000 people and infected tens of thousands since August, according to international health agencies. The disease has reached all of Zimbabwe’s provinces and spread into neighboring countries, including South Africa.

Hospitals and clinics are struggling with shortages of medicine, equipment and staff. In many communities, broken water systems and uncollected refuse have forced residents to draw drinking water from unsafe wells and streams. Aid organizations warn that the true number of cases may be higher than official figures because the health system can no longer reliably record infections.

The epidemic has intensified pressure on President Robert Mugabe, whose government says Western sanctions are chiefly responsible for Zimbabwe’s collapse. Critics instead blame years of economic mismanagement, political repression and the destruction of agricultural production.

Zimbabwe’s latest banknote, worth 10 billion Zimbabwe dollars, offers another stark measure of the crisis. Hyperinflation has made prices rise so rapidly that wages and bank withdrawals lose much of their value within days or even hours. Cash remains scarce despite the repeated introduction of higher-denomination notes, while many shops now demand payment in United States dollars or South African rand.

The turmoil follows a disputed election earlier this year. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai won more votes than Mr. Mugabe in the March presidential poll but, according to official results, fell short of the majority required to avoid a runoff. Mr. Tsvangirai withdrew from the June contest, citing widespread violence against his supporters, leaving Mr. Mugabe to claim victory in a vote condemned by many foreign governments.

Under a September agreement brokered by regional leaders, Mr. Mugabe was to remain president while Mr. Tsvangirai became prime minister in a unity government. The arrangement has stalled, however, amid disputes over control of key ministries, including home affairs, which oversees the police.

Opposition officials have also accused state security agencies of abducting activists, further eroding confidence in the agreement.

As the political impasse continues, ordinary Zimbabweans face severe food shortages, unemployment and the near-total breakdown of public services. Millions are believed to require food assistance, and large numbers have crossed into neighboring countries in search of work, medicine and basic supplies.

International officials warn that without urgent humanitarian aid and a functioning government, both the cholera epidemic and the wider national emergency are likely to worsen.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on claims that Zimbabwean children are “wasting away,” incorporating statistics on food insecurity, malnutrition, cholera deaths and infections, and the country’s population.
counterfactuals.output:
## Zimbabwe’s children and the “wasting away” claim

Claims that Zimbabwean children are “wasting away” reflect a genuine deterioration in nutrition during the El Niño-driven drought, although the phrase should not be interpreted as applying to every child.

- **Food insecurity:** Zimbabwe’s 2024 livelihood assessments projected that roughly **7.6–7.7 million people**—about **46% of the population**—would require food assistance during the January–March 2025 lean season. This included approximately **6 million rural residents** and **1.7 million people in urban areas**.
- **Child malnutrition:** The national rate of **acute malnutrition, or wasting, among children under five rose from about 2.8% to 4.9%**. In other words, roughly one in 20 young children surveyed had dangerously low weight for their height. About **23–24% of under-fives were stunted**, indicating long-term undernutrition.
- **Meaning of “wasting”:** In public-health terminology, wasting is a specific diagnosis based on low weight for height. Thus, reports of children “wasting away” have a factual basis, but the wording is broader and more dramatic than the statistics: most Zimbabwean children were not clinically wasted, while risks varied considerably by district.
- **Cholera:** The food crisis coincided with a major cholera outbreak. World Health Organization reporting through June 2024 recorded approximately **34,500 suspected infections and 718 associated deaths**. Only a portion were laboratory-confirmed, so reports citing much lower death totals—such as confirmed deaths alone—do not represent the full suspected outbreak toll.
- **Population:** Zimbabwe’s **2022 census counted about 15.18 million people**. UN and World Bank estimates for 2023–24 placed the population at roughly **16.3–16.6 million**, explaining why 7.6 million people is commonly described as “nearly half” the country.

Overall, the underlying emergency is well documented: drought, crop failure, high food prices and disease increased hunger and child malnutrition. The phrase “children are wasting away” is defensible as a description of affected children and the worsening trend, but it should not be read as a literal description of all Zimbabwean children.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed international news story from Harare explaining how Zimbabwe’s political crisis and economic collapse have led to shortages of food, medicine, fuel, cash, electricity, sanitation, and clean water.
counterfactuals.output:
**Zimbabwe’s political turmoil deepens a crisis of food, medicine and water**

**HARARE, Zimbabwe** — Before sunrise, residents carrying buckets gather around a public borehole in a crowded Harare township. The municipal taps have been dry for days, and the queue is already long. Nearby, rubbish lies uncollected beside an overflowing drain, while smoke from wood fires hangs over homes where electricity is available only intermittently.

Across Zimbabwe, the failure of basic services has become the most visible expression of a deeper national crisis. Years of disputed politics, weakening institutions, currency instability, drought and mismanagement have combined to leave many people struggling to obtain food, medicine, fuel, cash, electricity, sanitation and safe drinking water.

The collapse is not uniform. Imported groceries remain available in well-stocked supermarkets, private hospitals continue to serve those who can pay, and businesses with generators, solar panels and access to foreign currency can often keep operating. But for public-sector workers, pensioners, informal traders and unemployed families, daily life has become a search for essentials.

Zimbabwe’s political instability intensified after the military forced longtime ruler Robert Mugabe to resign in 2017. Emmerson Mnangagwa, Mugabe’s former deputy, promised economic recovery, international re-engagement and a break with the repression associated with the previous government. Instead, elections have remained bitterly contested, opposition activists have faced arrests and restrictions, and confidence in state institutions has continued to erode.

The governing ZANU-PF party says Western sanctions and recurring droughts have obstructed recovery. The United States and European governments have progressively changed or narrowed many of their sanctions, while maintaining measures aimed at particular officials or entities. Critics of the government argue that corruption, uncontrolled public spending, inconsistent economic policies and the suppression of political competition have done far greater damage.

The result is an economy in which prices can rise faster than wages and confidence in local money remains fragile. Zimbabwe has repeatedly introduced new currencies or monetary systems since the hyperinflation that destroyed the Zimbabwe dollar in 2008. Yet many citizens and businesses still prefer United States dollars for savings and major transactions.

For workers paid mainly in local currency, that creates a punishing gap. Salaries lose purchasing power, while landlords, pharmacies, transport operators and some retailers seek payment in hard currency. Official exchange rates have often diverged from rates in the informal market, encouraging speculation and making it difficult for businesses to plan.

Cash itself can be scarce. Banks and automated teller machines may not provide enough physical notes, forcing people to rely on electronic payments, mobile money or informal currency dealers. Transaction charges and exchange-rate losses reduce already meagre incomes.

Food is among the most urgent concerns. Poor harvests linked to drought, high prices for seed and fertiliser, and the disruption of commercial agriculture have increased dependence on imports and food aid. Maize meal, the main ingredient in Zimbabwe’s staple dish, can become unaffordable even when it is available. Meat, cooking oil and bread are beyond the regular reach of many low-income households.

Families respond by reducing the number of meals they eat, buying food in tiny quantities or replacing more nutritious products with cheaper starches. In rural districts, failed crops and depleted livestock leave households dependent on government distribution programmes and international aid agencies. In cities, hunger is less visible but widespread, concealed behind closed doors as families stretch one meal across an entire day.

Zimbabwe’s health system reflects the same breakdown. Public hospitals and clinics frequently face shortages of medicines, laboratory supplies, protective equipment and functioning machinery. Patients may be given prescriptions and told to purchase drugs from private pharmacies, where prices are often quoted in United States dollars.

Doctors and nurses have repeatedly protested over low pay and poor working conditions. Skilled medical professionals continue to leave for jobs abroad, deepening staff shortages. Even where treatment is officially subsidised, patients may have to provide gloves, syringes or dressings themselves.

Power cuts make the situation more dangerous. Hospitals require electricity for operating theatres, oxygen systems, laboratories, refrigeration and maternity wards. Backup generators help only when fuel is available and affordable.

Zimbabwe depends heavily on hydropower from the Kariba complex, which is vulnerable to low water levels, as well as ageing coal-fired plants that frequently suffer breakdowns. When domestic production falls short, the country must import electricity, but utilities struggling with debt and foreign-currency shortages cannot always secure enough power.

Blackouts can last for much of the day. Small companies lose production, food spoils in refrigerators, mobile-phone networks weaken and children study by candlelight. Those who can afford solar equipment or diesel generators have created private alternatives, widening the divide between protected households and everyone else.

Fuel supplies have periodically been disrupted by a shortage of foreign currency and delayed imports. Long queues can form when petrol or diesel becomes scarce. Higher fuel prices quickly spread through the economy, raising the cost of commuter transport, farming, food distribution and generator use.

Water shortages are particularly acute in Harare and other cities. Municipal authorities struggle to maintain ageing pipes, pumping stations and treatment plants. The cost of imported purification chemicals, electricity cuts and declining revenue all limit the amount of treated water that can be delivered.

In some neighbourhoods, residents go for days or weeks without reliable tap water. They turn to shallow wells, private vendors and crowded boreholes. Water purchased from tankers is too expensive for many families, while unsafe sources expose communities to cholera, typhoid and other waterborne diseases.

Sanitation deteriorates alongside the water system. Toilets cannot be flushed, sewage pipes burst, and uncollected rubbish blocks drains. During the rainy season, contaminated water can flow into wells and densely populated settlements. Public-health campaigns urging people to wash their hands carry little meaning where soap and clean water are scarce.

Local governments say they lack the money to repair infrastructure, while residents argue that they cannot pay higher rates for services they do not receive. The conflict creates a cycle of falling revenue and worsening provision.

Zimbabwe’s crisis has been compounded by its international isolation and heavy debt burden. Arrears to global lenders have limited access to affordable long-term financing. Attempts to restore relations with creditors have repeatedly stalled over demands for political reform, compensation for past land seizures, economic transparency and improved respect for human rights.

The government points to new roads, mining investment and infrastructure projects as evidence of progress. Gold, platinum, lithium and tobacco continue to generate export earnings. But critics say the benefits are concentrated among politically connected elites and do not translate into reliable public services.

The mining sector also presents a stark contradiction: Zimbabwe is rich in natural resources, yet the state often lacks the foreign currency required to import medicines, electricity, fuel and water-treatment chemicals. Questions over opaque contracts, illicit financial flows and corruption have reinforced public suspicion that national wealth is being diverted.

Political repression further complicates the search for solutions. Opposition groups and civil-society organisations say restrictions on demonstrations, arrests of activists and pressure on independent media reduce the space for public debate. The authorities maintain that they are enforcing the law and protecting stability.

For many Zimbabweans, however, politics is inseparable from survival. A disputed election can weaken investor confidence; a sudden currency directive can erase wages; a crackdown can shut informal markets; and a failure to maintain a power plant can stop water pumps across an entire city.

The burden falls most heavily on women, who often spend hours searching for water, food and medicine, and on children, whose education is disrupted by power cuts, hunger and disease. Pensioners who worked for decades can find their savings reduced to almost nothing by inflation and currency changes.

Migration has become another coping mechanism. Millions of Zimbabweans are believed to live and work abroad, especially in South Africa, Britain and Botswana. Their remittances support households and provide vital foreign currency, but the exodus has deprived the country of teachers, nurses, engineers and other skilled workers.

Back at the borehole in Harare, the line advances slowly. Residents fill every container they can carry because no one knows when water will next be available. Similar calculations take place across the country: whether to buy food or medicine, pay for transport or save for school fees, charge a phone or preserve a small solar battery for the night.

Zimbabwe’s emergency is therefore not a single shortage but a chain of interconnected failures. Currency instability makes imports more expensive. Fuel shortages disrupt transport and generators. Power cuts stop pumps and hospitals. Water failures fuel disease. Medicine shortages make those diseases more deadly. Political mistrust and weak institutions make each problem harder to solve.

For citizens who have endured decades of economic shocks, the crisis is measured less in official statistics than in hours spent queueing — for bread, petrol, cash, medicine and water — and in the growing number of basic services that must now be secured privately in a country where most people cannot afford them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
